name: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia

clinicalPearls: DIPNECH is a generalised proliferation of pulmonary neuroendocrine cells confined to the airway epithelium and is regarded by the WHO as a preinvasive lesion for carcinoid tumours.
It predominantly affects middle-aged and older women, frequently lifelong non-smokers.
The usual presentation is chronic cough with slowly progressive breathlessness, and patients are often labelled asthmatic for years before diagnosis.
The combination on HRCT of mosaic attenuation with expiratory air trapping plus multiple small nodules (tumourlets or carcinoids) is highly suggestive.
Physiology is characteristically obstructive, reflecting an associated constrictive (obliterative) bronchiolitis, rather than restrictive.
Somatostatin-receptor imaging (for example gallium-DOTATATE PET or an octreotide scan) can highlight the neuroendocrine nodules.
When a neuroendocrine nest breaches the basement membrane it is termed a tumourlet, and a larger lesion beyond an arbitrary size threshold is classified as a carcinoid tumour.
Somatostatin analogues may relieve symptoms in progressive disease, while otherwise management is supportive with imaging surveillance for carcinoid growth.
reference.pathophysiology: DIPNECH is characterised by a widespread increase in pulmonary neuroendocrine cells, appearing as scattered single cells, small clusters and linear proliferations, all confined within the bronchial and bronchiolar epithelium with an intact basement membrane. When these cells breach the basement membrane but remain small they are called tumourlets, and larger nodular proliferations are classified as carcinoid tumours, placing DIPNECH at the origin of a preinvasive-to-invasive neuroendocrine sequence. The neuroendocrine cells secrete bioactive peptides such as gastrin-releasing peptide (bombesin) and other mediators that are thought to promote peribronchiolar fibrosis, producing a constrictive bronchiolitis with airflow obstruction and air trapping. It arises predominantly in middle-aged and older women, often non-smokers, and the precise molecular drivers remain uncertain, although it is frequently discovered incidentally in lung tissue resected for a carcinoid tumour.
additionalDifferentials: Asthma or other obstructive airways disease
Multiple pulmonary metastases or nodules of other aetiology
Typical or atypical carcinoid tumour arising without background DIPNECH
Miliary infection such as tuberculosis or other granulomatous disease
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution CT of the chest with an expiratory phase (mosaic attenuation, air trapping and nodules)
Pulmonary function tests showing an obstructive pattern with air trapping and often reduced gas transfer
Somatostatin-receptor imaging (gallium-DOTATATE PET or octreotide scan)
Surgical lung biopsy with neuroendocrine immunohistochemistry (chromogranin, synaptophysin, CD56)
Urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid if features of carcinoid syndrome are present
Serial imaging surveillance for growth of nodules
Bronchoscopy where a central endobronchial lesion is suspected
redFlags: An enlarging nodule or a new dominant mass, indicating progression to a carcinoid tumour
Symptoms of carcinoid syndrome such as flushing, diarrhoea and wheeze
Rapidly progressive airflow obstruction or respiratory failure
Hepatic or nodal lesions suggesting metastatic carcinoid
reference.prognosis: The disorder is generally indolent with slow progression; airflow obstruction may worsen over years, and although associated carcinoids are usually low-grade, a minority develop clinically significant or metastatic neuroendocrine tumours, so long-term surveillance is warranted.
pitfalls: Prolonged misdiagnosis as asthma or COPD, delaying recognition for years.
Overlooking DIPNECH when it is found incidentally in tissue around a resected carcinoid.
Interpreting multiple lung nodules as metastatic malignancy without considering tumourlets.
Expecting a restrictive picture, when the physiology is characteristically obstructive.
Attributing mosaic attenuation solely to primary small-airways or pulmonary vascular disease.
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
